lead: A Raspberry Pi is a small single-board computer. It runs Linux from a microSD card, so it has a file system, user accounts and a terminal, not just one repeating program. A 40-pin header exposes general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins at 3.3 V logic. That mix makes the Pi useful when an IoT node must sense, decide, log data and serve a web page, while still driving simple LEDs, relays and sensors. This chapter looks at the board blocks, the Linux system that starts on power-up, and the serial interfaces UART, I2C, SPI and PWM.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 on single-board computers and Chapter 4.1 for the contrast with a microcontroller board; basic Linux helps.

sections.h3: Board blocks and the 3.3 V header

blocks.text: A Raspberry Pi board is built around a system on chip (SoC). The SoC contains the processor, graphics unit, memory controller and many peripherals on one integrated circuit. RAM (random-access memory) chips sit beside it and hold running programs; RAM loses its contents when power is removed. A microSD card holds the operating system and files, so it is non-volatile storage.

The board also has USB ports, an HDMI video output, and Ethernet or Wi-Fi for network access. The 40-pin GPIO header is the part an IoT circuit uses. GPIO means general-purpose input/output: pins that software can set high or low, or read as high or low.

Logic level is the voltage that represents 0 or 1. On the Raspberry Pi header, high is 3.3 V and low is 0 V. A pin is not 5 V tolerant. A 5 V signal connected directly to a GPIO pin can damage the SoC. Use a level shifter or a resistor divider when a sensor outputs 5 V. Some header pins also carry UART, I2C, SPI and PWM signals.

sections.h3: Linux boot, user account, terminal, apt and files

blocks.text: On power-up, the Raspberry Pi reads a bootloader from the microSD card. The bootloader loads the Linux kernel into RAM. The kernel is the core of the operating system; it talks to hardware and starts services. The kernel mounts the root file system from the microSD card. A login prompt then appears. Some syllabi call the standard system Raspberry Pi OS, formerly Raspbian.

A user account separates your files and permissions from system files. The terminal is a text interface: you type a command, press Enter, and read the output. Common file commands are ls to list a directory, cd to change directory, and nano to edit a text file. Your home directory is usually /home/username.

The package manager apt installs software. The command sudo apt update refreshes the package list; sudo runs the command as the superuser. The command sudo apt install package-name installs a package and its dependencies. Reboot after a kernel update. A Pi can also run a web server or an MQTT client, so it can act as a small network node, not only as a local controller.

sections.h3: Interfaces: UART, I2C, SPI and PWM

blocks.text: The header exposes several serial interfaces. UART means universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter. It uses two data wires, TX and RX, and no shared clock. Both ends must use the same baud rate, which is bits per second. UART is point-to-point.

I2C means inter-integrated circuit. It uses two wires, SDA for data and SCL for clock. Many devices share the bus, and each device has a 7-bit address. Pull-up resistors are needed on both lines. SPI means serial peripheral interface. It uses SCLK for clock, MOSI for master-out-slave-in, MISO for master-in-slave-out, and one chip-select (CS) line per device. SPI is faster than I2C but uses more pins.
PWM means pulse-width modulation. A pin switches fast between high and low. Duty cycle is the fraction of time the pin is high:

blocks.text: PWM sets LED brightness or motor speed. All these signals use 3.3 V logic on the Pi. A 5 V device needs a level shifter. Sensor wiring is in Chapter 4.5; Python control is in Chapter 4.4.

examples.question: A red LED with forward voltage 2.0 V is driven from a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin whose high level is 3.3 V. The design target is 5 mA. Find the exact series resistance, choose the nearest standard value, and find the actual current. State units.
steps: GPIO high voltage is 3.3 V, LED forward voltage is 2.0 V, target current is 5 mA = 0.005 A.
260 Ω is not a standard value; the nearest standard value is 270 Ω.
Actual current = 1.3 V ÷ 270 Ω = 0.00481 A = 4.81 mA.
examples.answer: The exact resistance is 260 Ω; use 270 Ω, giving an actual current of 4.81 mA.
examples.check:
v_gpio = 3.3
v_led = 2.0
i_target_a = 0.005
r_exact = (v_gpio - v_led) / i_target_a
r_standard = 270
i_actual_a = (v_gpio - v_led) / r_standard
i_actual_ma = i_actual_a * 1000
print(r_exact)
print(r_standard)
print(round(i_actual_ma, 2))

traps: Raspberry Pi GPIO is 3.3 V logic and not 5 V tolerant; a 5 V sensor output can damage the pin unless you use a level shifter or divider.
Do not confuse RAM with microSD: RAM is volatile working memory; the OS and files live on the microSD card.
UART has no shared clock and is point-to-point; I2C is an addressed bus with SDA and SCL; SPI uses chip-select lines.
Duty cycle and frequency are different: duty cycle sets the high-time fraction, frequency sets how many periods occur per second.
In the LED resistor calculation, convert mA to A before dividing; 5 mA is 0.005 A. The exact 260 Ω is not standard; 270 Ω gives 4.81 mA.

quiz.q: What is an SoC on a Raspberry Pi board?
quiz.a: A system on chip: one integrated circuit holding the processor, graphics unit, memory controller and many peripherals.

quiz.q: What is stored on the microSD card, and why is it needed?
quiz.a: The operating system and user files are stored there. It is non-volatile, so it keeps data when power is removed.

quiz.q: Why is a 5 V sensor output dangerous to a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin?
quiz.a: The GPIO high level is 3.3 V and the pin is not 5 V tolerant. A 5 V input can damage the SoC. Use a level shifter or resistor divider.

quiz.q: An LED has forward voltage 1.8 V and is driven from a 3.3 V Raspberry Pi GPIO at a target current of 10 mA. Find the exact series resistance and the nearest standard value, then find the current with 150 Ω.
quiz.a: Resistor voltage = 3.3 V − 1.8 V = 1.5 V. Target current = 10 mA = 0.010 A. R = 1.5 V ÷ 0.010 A = 150 Ω, which is standard. Actual current = 1.5 V ÷ 150 Ω = 0.010 A = 10 mA.

quiz.q: Two I2C sensors on the same bus have the same 7-bit address. What problem occurs, and what is one fix?
quiz.a: The master cannot select one sensor uniquely, so reads may clash. Use an I2C multiplexer, or change one sensor to a different address if it supports that.

quiz.q: You must log a temperature value every minute to a file and serve a small web page. Why is a Raspberry Pi a better fit than a basic Arduino board for this task?
quiz.a: The Pi runs Linux, so it has a file system, network services and a web server. An Arduino runs one repeating program and lacks a full OS and file system.

quiz.q: A Raspberry Pi resets when a DC motor starts, although it works on the bench. Give a likely cause and a fix.
quiz.a: The motor inrush current causes a supply voltage dip or electrical noise. Use a separate motor supply and a motor driver, add decoupling, and keep a common ground.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production Raspberry Pi systems often use read-only root file systems, container images and remote update tools so a power cut does not corrupt the microSD card. Device tree overlays describe how Linux should map header pins to drivers, which matters when one board model changes its pin functions. Real-time Linux patches and external microcontrollers are used when a motor or sensor needs microsecond timing. Search next: Raspberry Pi device tree overlay, Linux GPIO character device, PREEMPT_RT, and balena or Mender for fleet updates.
